title: Not Until the Evidence Says So: Teaching LLM Investigators When to Close a Case

paper.title: Not Until the Evidence Says So: Teaching LLM Investigators When to Close a Case
paper.abstract:
Abstract Accident, defect and outage investigations end with a decision that ordinary question answering never faces: whether the evidence gathered so far is enough to close the case.
We study this decision for LLM investigators, which request evidence from a case file, revise their hypotheses, and either close the case with a conclusion grounded in what they read or leave it open and name what is missing.
This judgment does not come with capability: an untrained 9B model overstates its evidence in 97% of its answers, and a frontier model that identifies the right cause in 84% of cases still overstates in 91% and closes 17 of the 41 cases whose official finding is “cause undetermined”.
Measuring it is also non-trivial: the source of a case largely predicts its label, and a rule that reads only the source reaches 83.0 balanced accuracy on our test cases.
We therefore evaluate closure with three tests: closure accuracy , reported against this rule and within each source; evidence dependence , which removes the grounds of a conclusion and checks whether the model stops closing; and conclusion and gap quality , a judged checklist of what the model asserts and what it says is missing.
We build Nautil, 731 audited cases from aviation, rail, maritime, chemical-safety and vehicle-defect reports and production server incidents, with teacher trajectories, an out-of-distribution test set and counterfactual evidence versions.
Fine-tuning a 9B model on these trajectories makes its closures follow the evidence: removing the grounds lowers its closure rate by 26 points relative to a matched control (base model: 6; frontier model: 7), overstatement falls from 97% to 35%, and conclusions that are both correct and not overstated rise from 3% to 43% (frontier model: 9%).
Reinforcement learning that rewards only the closure decision then raises balanced accuracy from 69.2 to 83.3, on par with the teacher, and within-source accuracy from 60.4 to 74.1, at some cost in evidence dependence.
We release the models, the dataset and the evaluation suite.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: Three investigators on a test case whose official finding is a partial loss of engine power for undetermined reasons . Left: the untrained base model turns an unverified reading into an established engine failure and closes the case. Middle: a frontier model names the power loss that the report establishes and even writes that its cause could not be determined, yet still closes the case. Right: Nautil-SFT keeps the case open and names the missing evidence. Excerpts are the models’ own words, shortened (…); one sample per model. Investigating an aircraft accident, a vehicle defect or a server outage means collecting evidence piece by piece and then deciding whether it is enough to state a cause. Official investigations often decide that it is not: many reports end with “cause undetermined”. An LLM investigator therefore has to make two decisions, not one: what the cause is, and whether the evidence at hand establishes it. Current models are much better at the first decision than at the second (Figure 1 ). On our test cases, a frontier model (Gemini 3.8 Flash) identifies the reference cause in 84% of cases, yet 91% of its answers present as established what the evidence only suggests, and it closes 17 of the 41 cases that the official reports leave undetermined. An untrained 9B model overstates in 97% of its answers. Knowing when to close does not come with the ability to find causes; it has to be taught and measured separately. Abstention research asks whether to answer a single question whose information is given up front ( Kirichenko et al., 2025 ; Zhai et al., 2026 ) , and diagnosis agents are scored on finding the cause ( Xu et al., 2025 ; Pham et al., 2025 ) , not on whether they should have concluded. Our cases hold tens to hundreds of evidence items that must be requested over several turns, and “the cause cannot be determined from this record” is a correct, scored outcome. Measuring this decision is harder than it looks. In real investigation data the source of a case largely predicts its label: most NTSB and NHTSA cases in our data end undetermined, most board and server cases end with a cause. A rule that ignores the evidence and answers by source reaches 83.0 balanced accuracy on our non-host test cases. Any closure accuracy on such data must therefore be read against this rule, within each source, and together with tests that change the evidence while keeping the source fixed. We make four contributions. • Task and evaluation. We define investigative closure and evaluate it with three complementary tests: closure accuracy (reported against the source-only rule and within each source), evidence dependence (counterfactual removal of a conclusion’s grounds against a matched control), and conclusion and gap quality (a judged checklist). • Data. Nautil 1 1 1 Read as not until . contains 731 audited cases from four sources, including real production server incidents, with teacher investigation trajectories, a 141-case out-of-distribution test set and counterfactual evidence versions. • Models. Nautil-SFT and Nautil-RLVR, two 9B investigators. Supervised fine-tuning on audited trajectories makes closure follow the evidence and cuts overstatement; reinforcement learning with a reward on the closure decision alone raises closure accuracy to the teacher’s level. • Findings. Training teaches restraint and grounding rather than cause-finding; rewarding judged conclusion quality during RL collapses the policy into never closing; and an outcome-only reward trades evidence dependence for accuracy.

sections.heading: Abstention and unanswerable questions.
sections.text: Models answer questions they cannot answer ( Rajpurkar et al., 2018 ; Yin et al., 2023 ; Kadavath et al., 2022 ) , even when the context is insufficient ( Joren et al., 2025 ; Kirichenko et al., 2025 ) , partly because binary grading rewards guessing ( Kalai et al., 2025 ) . Abstention has been trained with SFT ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024 ) and RL ( Wei et al., 2026 ; Damani et al., 2026 ; Zhai et al., 2026 ) ; RL fine-tuning can also erode it ( Song et al., 2025b ) , and abstention rewards can collapse into refusal ( Che et al., 2026 ) . Recent work asks models to state what is missing ( Zhai et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2025 ) or to stop acting when they should ( Liu et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . These settings give the information up front and grade whether to answer; in ours, the decision follows multi-turn evidence gathering, and “cannot determine” is set by real investigation reports.

sections.heading: LLMs for incident investigation and diagnosis.
sections.text: Root-cause analysis benchmarks and agents for cloud incidents ( Xu et al., 2025 ; Pham et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) , auditable multi-agent diagnosis such as JustDiag ( Bi et al., 2026 ) , evidence-first investigators ( Marozzo and Liò, 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) , and sequential medical diagnosis ( Nori et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2024 ) all score whether the cause is found. Premature closure has been measured in frontier models ( Handler et al., 2026 ) . We add closure itself as a scored, trainable decision across domains.

sections.heading: RLVR and agentic RL.
sections.text: Group-relative policy optimisation ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) and tool-using RL agents ( Jin et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2025a ; Wang et al., 2025 ) assume a solvable task with a checkable answer. We make “not closed” one of the verifiable outcomes and show that judge-scored rubric rewards ( Gunjal et al., 2026 ) , which can be gamed ( Skalse et al., 2022 ; Gao et al., 2023 ) , collapse closure in this setting.

sections.heading: Shortcuts and faithful evaluation.
sections.text: Annotation artefacts and shortcuts let models score without using the input ( Gururangan et al., 2018 ; Geirhos et al., 2020 ) ; contrast sets and counterfactual edits test whether predictions follow it ( Gardner et al., 2020 ; Kaushik et al., 2020 ) , though constructed insufficiency has its own artefacts ( Qiu et al., 2026 ) . LLM judges are useful but biased, including towards their own outputs ( Zheng et al., 2023 ; Panickssery et al., 2024 ) . These motivate our source-only baseline, matched control and cross-judge checks.

sections.heading: Protocol.
sections.text: An investigator receives a case: a fixed question (what caused the incident, citing evidence for each key claim), a brief, an opening record E 1 E_{1} shown in full (median 4 items), and an index that lists only the identifier and a neutral title of every other evidence item (over all 731 cases: median 115 items per case, up to 682). Titles are written so that they do not reveal conclusions. In each turn the investigator writes a working note (current hypotheses, what the new evidence supports or weakens, a hypothesis ledger, and the next discriminating check) and may call request_evidence for 1–12 unread items; the items arrive in the next message. An episode has at most 15 turns and ends with an answer that starts with case closed , followed by a causal conclusion that cites the evidence, or case not closed , followed by what is established, what is missing, and a provisional assessment. The label of a report case is whether the official report determined the cause at the level its investigation pursued (the closure object in the reference); a report that establishes an event, such as a loss of engine power, but not its cause leaves the case open.

sections.heading: Three tests.
sections.text: A single accuracy can be inflated either by the source of a case or by a conservative policy, so we evaluate closure with three tests, each closing one loophole: closure accuracy guards against recognising the source instead of reading the evidence; evidence dependence guards against closing out of habit, or stopping merely because evidence is scarce; and conclusion and gap quality guards against a right decision with a wrong or overstated conclusion. Closure accuracy. We report the rate of closing among cases that should close, the rate of not closing among cases that should not, and their mean (balanced accuracy), so that never closing is not rewarded. An answer without a closure marker counts as wrong on both sides. Every result is shown next to the source-only rule , which gives each source its majority training label. Within-source balanced accuracy computes balanced accuracy separately inside each report source and averages them; the source-only rule scores exactly 50 on it, so only reading the evidence can raise it. Evidence dependence. For cases labelled closed, we build a version without the items the conclusion rests on and a control without the same number of other items; the brief and question are unchanged, and removed items simply drop out of the index. The two versions differ only in whether the grounds are present, so the source is held fixed. We report the difference in closure rate between them (removed minus control; more negative means closure follows the evidence) and a two-class balanced accuracy per case, 1 2 ​ [ 𝟙 ​ ( control closed ) + 𝟙 ​ ( removed explicitly not closed ) ] \tfrac{1}{2}[\mathbb{1}(\text{control closed})+\mathbb{1}(\text{removed explicitly not closed})] . Conclusion and gap quality. A judge answers a fixed checklist about the final answer against the reference: whether the initiating cause is right, whether the causal chain matches, whether the answer overstates (presents as established what the evidence only suggests), what share of its causal claims cite evidence that was read and supports them, and whether it addresses alternative explanations. Our summary metric is the share of answers whose cause is right and not overstated. For unclosed answers the judge also checks whether the gap names specific evidence, whether that evidence is truly absent from the case, and whether it matches the reference’s reason for indeterminacy. The main judge is GPT-6 Sol; because it is also the teacher (§ 4 ), we repeat the checklist with Claude Sonnet 5 and Grok 4.7 (§ 6.3 , Appendix C ).

sections.heading: 4 The Nautil Dataset
sections.text: Figure 2: Overview of Nautil. (1) Case files are built from four sources: evidence items with neutral titles are shown on demand, conclusions are withheld, and a hidden reference records whether the case should close; counterfactual versions and the OOD set follow the same format. (2) The teacher plans each investigation from the report and its label, a program assembles and checks it, Stage 2 adds citations and the hypothesis ledger, and audited trajectories train Nautil-SFT. (3) RLVR rewards only the closure decision, checked by a program. Right: one round of an actual Nautil-SFT investigation on a test case whose official finding is undetermined; after its checks weaken the fuel and engine explanations, it leaves the case open.

sections.heading: Sources.
sections.text: Nautil draws on four kinds of investigation (Table 1 ). Boards : reports of four transport and chemical-safety boards (ATSB, RAIB, MAIB, CSB). NTSB : aviation final reports 2014–2024. NHTSA : vehicle defect investigations, with opening and closing summaries. Host : anomaly windows from a year of production server monitoring at a large internet company. Report cases take their label from whether the official report determined the cause. Host incidents have no report; their label is the teacher’s closure decision (below), which we use for training and report only in the appendix.

sections.heading: Case files.
sections.text: For reports, an extraction pipeline (GPT-5.6 Sol) splits the text into factual, analytical and conclusion passages, turns factual passages into atomic evidence items with neutral titles, withholds any sentence that hints at the conclusion, writes the brief, anonymises identifiers, and records a hidden reference: whether the cause was determined, the official conclusion, rejected explanations and alternatives left open. E 1 E_{1} is fixed to the first four observation or measurement items of the primary source. For hosts, selected metric series are rendered as charts and described in text by a vision-language model that sees each chart with its numbers table and may quote only those numbers; a program flags any number not in the table. Service names are replaced by neutral roles, and addresses, alert IDs and dates are removed.

sections.heading: Teacher trajectories.
sections.text: The teacher (GPT-6 Sol) sees the case file, the official analysis and the label, and plans an investigation: per turn, a note, the items to request and why, then a final answer (Stage 1). A program assembles the dialogue with tool returns copied verbatim, rejecting plans that cite unrequested items, contradict the label or leak withheld identifiers. Stage 2 adds exact citations and a ledger marking each hypothesis open, favoured or weakened, with every change citing visible evidence. For hosts the teacher also sees the closing report of a run of the JustDiag diagnostic harness ( Bi et al., 2026 ) on the incident. Trajectories are retraced from the report’s argument; their fetch order is not free exploration.

sections.heading: Audit.
sections.text: The teacher scores each trajectory from − 5 -5 to + 5 +5 on alignment with the source, evidence grounding, active fetching, hypothesis updates and honest closure; we keep scores ≥ 4 \geq 4 without hard failures and allow one revision of the final answer for + 3 +3 . Of 1,345 generated report and host cases, 996 pass Stage 1, 818 pass Stage 2 and 518 (38.5%) pass the audit; with supplements for host not-closed cases, a salvage round and the removal of 26 cases whose brief and evidence came from different incidents, the final set has 731 cases. It is split 545 / 74 / 112 within each source, balancing labels and keeping each incident in one split. Table 1: Nautil by source. Items: median evidence items per case, over all cases of the source. sections.heading: Source and label.
sections.text: Table 1 shows the structure that makes closure hard to measure: boards and hosts mostly close, NTSB and NHTSA mostly do not. Answering by source alone gives 83.0 balanced accuracy on the 64 non-host test cases (23 should close, 41 should not). This is why every closure result below is paired with the source-only rule and the within-source metric, and why the headline test set is non-host: host labels are teacher judgments, and the teacher itself, rerun under the same protocol, closes only 5 of the 39 host test cases labelled closed.

sections.heading: Out-of-distribution test set.
sections.text: 141 cases from unseen domains: 83 reports (NTSB highway and pipeline, TSB Canada pipeline), 20 medical cases ( Wu et al., 2025 ) relabelled by whether the record contains the confirming finding, 18 microservice faults ( Pham et al., 2025 ) , and 20 Tennessee Eastman process runs ( Downs and Vogel, 1993 ; Rieth et al., 2017 ) . Domain and label are again tied, so we report the OOD set per domain and as a secondary column.

sections.heading: Counterfactual versions.
sections.text: For the 62 test cases the teacher closes, the grounds are the items its final answer cites; versions remove 40%, 75% or 100% of them, and the control removes as many other items. A leak check flags removed items that may be restated elsewhere; 20 cases have none.

sections.heading: Supervised fine-tuning.
sections.text: We fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B ( Qwen Team, 2026 ) with LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) (rank 16, α = 32 \alpha=32 , all linear layers) on the 545 training trajectories, with the native tool-call format, a 32k-token context, and loss on assistant turns only. We train two epochs (546 steps) and select the epoch-2 checkpoint before touching the test set: validation loss flattens after it, validation closure accuracy is highest, and its samples disagree most on the closure decision, which leaves room for RL. We call it Nautil-SFT.

sections.heading: RLVR with a closure-only reward.
sections.text: Starting from Nautil-SFT, we run GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) in the same case environment. The reward is deliberately simple and fully checked by a program: r = D + s , D = { + 1 closure decision matches the label , − 1 it does not, or no closure marker , r=D+s,\qquad D=\begin{cases}+1&\text{closure decision matches the label},\\ -1&\text{it does not, or no closure marker},\end{cases} (1) where s ≤ 0 s\leq 0 is a format penalty (no citation in the final answer, citing unread or non-existent items, turns beyond six, repeated requests, malformed calls, a missing marker). Within each group, s s is centred separately among closing and non-closing rollouts, so that only D D separates the two decisions. No judge is called during training. Cases are drawn uniformly from the eight source × \times label strata, so that no source dominates the updates; host cases, whose labels are teacher judgments, make up a quarter of the draws. Each step samples 22 cases with 8 rollouts each (temperature 1.0, up to 15 turns); we use learning rate 5 × 10 − 6 5\times 10^{-6} , asymmetric clipping (0.2 / 0.28) ( Yu et al., 2025 ) , no KL term, and 50 steps on two H100 GPUs. We select step 30 as Nautil-RLVR with a screening evaluation that included 30 test cases (22 of them non-host); Appendix B reports results with those cases removed. We arrived at this reward after two judge-based variants performed worse (§ 6.4 ); full settings are in Appendix B .

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: All investigators run the same protocol, prompt and tool. We compare the untrained base model (Qwen3.5-9B), the base model prompted with ReAct ( Yao et al., 2023 ) or with our note-and-ledger format, Abstain-R1 ( Zhai et al., 2026 ) and its 3B base model, Gemini 3.8 Flash as a frontier model, Nautil-SFT, Nautil-RLVR, and GPT-6 Sol as a teacher reference. 9B and 3B models are sampled three times per case; API models once, except Gemini on the non-host counterfactual cases (three times). Unless noted, numbers are on the 64 non-host test cases, averaged over samples per case; intervals and host results are in Appendix D .

Yes: training turns a model that closes almost everything into one that separates the two kinds of case, and not only by source (Table 2 ). The base model closes 81% of cases that should close but leaves only 18.7% of undetermined cases open, for 49.9 balanced accuracy. Nautil-SFT leaves 93.5% of undetermined cases open, the highest of all models, and reaches 69.2; Nautil-RLVR balances both sides (81.2 / 85.4) and reaches 83.3, on par with the teacher (81.8) and Gemini (79.3). Gemini reaches its score by closing every case that should close and 41% of those that should not. Within each source, where the source-only rule is at 50, Nautil-RLVR reaches 74.1 (Nautil-SFT 60.4, base 48.2), so its gains come from separating cases of the same source. Gemini’s 77.0 is helped by NHTSA and NTSB having only 2 and 3 should-close cases; on boards, the only source with enough cases on both sides, Nautil-RLVR reaches 78.7, Gemini 70.0 and Nautil-SFT 70.2 (differences within noise). Over the whole test set, Nautil-RLVR ties the source-only rule (83.3 vs. 83.0), which is why the next two tests matter. The Nautil-SFT numbers are unaffected by checkpoint selection; the Nautil-RLVR checkpoint was screened on a set that included 22 of the 64 test cases (Appendix B ).

Overstatement falls from 97% (base) to 35% (Nautil-SFT); the share of causal claims backed by evidence the model actually read rises from 26% to 78%; and answers that are both right about the cause and not overstated rise from 3% to 43%, against 9% for Gemini. Overstatement rates depend on the judge (Sonnet 5: 11% for Nautil-SFT, 55% for Gemini), but the ranking holds, and all three judges find trained models overstate far less (Appendix C ). The limitation is on the other side of the decision: when Nautil-SFT leaves a case open, its gap is often generic (gap score 0.38 against Gemini’s 0.96), naming the specific missing evidence in 32% of unclosed answers.

Without them, the model never leaves a case open (0.0%) and overstates in 84% of its answers (Table 5 ). Without the hypothesis ledger, closure depends less on the evidence. Removing it leaves accuracy slightly higher but within noise of Nautil-SFT (76.3 vs. 69.2), while the counterfactual effect shrinks from − - 26.1 to − - 8.7; the difference is clear on all 62 cases, and its interval reaches zero on the 23 non-host cases. Data scale matters: 10%, 50% and 100% of the trajectories give 45.9, 64.9 and 69.2 (the number of steps grows with the data). A closure-only reward gives the largest and cleanest RL gain. It raises balanced accuracy by 14.1 points and within-source accuracy from 60.4 to 74.1, removes missing closure markers (5.2% to 0), and shortens investigations (5.5 to 4.6 turns); the OOD gain (5.3 points) is within noise. Adding the judged checklist to the reward is harmful: counted on every rollout, it drives the policy towards never closing (17.4% of should-close cases closed at step 10); counted only when the decision is right, it avoids the collapse but gains only 3.8 points. A likely reason: when every rollout in a group is wrong, the checklist still ranks the wrong answers, and this spills over into reluctance to close. The closure-only reward has a measurable cost: the counterfactual effect shrinks ( − - 26.1 to − - 15.9; − - 23.3 to − - 5.0 without leaks), addressing alternatives drops (38% to 17%), and the conclusion score falls by 0.05: a trade-off between accuracy and evidence dependence, with Nautil-SFT and Nautil-RLVR at its two ends.

sections.heading: Prompting and single-turn abstention training do not substitute.
sections.text: ReAct prompting (47.7) and our ledger format as a prompt (55.3, with 95% overstatement) leave the base model’s closing habit intact (Table 2 ). Abstain-R1 (27.9) and its base model (39.2) mostly fail to finish a multi-turn investigation (44% and 32% of runs end without a closure marker): abstention learned on single questions does not carry over to evidence gathering.

sections.heading: Out of distribution and long files.
sections.text: OOD balanced accuracy rises from 50.6 (base) to 61.7 (Nautil-SFT) and 67.0 (Nautil-RLVR), close to Gemini (68.9). Because domain and label are tied in this set, this mostly reflects the direction of the decision; within individual domains no model is clearly above chance (Appendix D ). On the 20 largest files, Nautil-RLVR closes 93% of should-close cases when fetching its own evidence and 61% when given the whole file, which in turn matches the main cause more often (Appendix E ). Appendix Figure 7 shows a failure in which Nautil-SFT misreads a valve test.

sections.heading: 7 Limitations
sections.text: Labels and sources. The source of a case still predicts its label, so accuracy is paired with within-source and counterfactual tests; the within-source metric rests mostly on board cases. Host labels are teacher judgments the teacher does not reproduce; host results are in the appendix. Judge, teacher and samples. GPT-6 Sol is both teacher and main judge, so its investigator row is only a reference; two further judges agree on direction but not on absolute rates. API models are mostly sampled once; the non-host counterfactual set has 23 cases, and its grounds are defined by the teacher’s citations. The Nautil-RLVR checkpoint was screened on 30 test cases, and a 33-case pilot set consulted while choosing the SFT epoch overlaps the OOD test set. Data. About 4% of references have extraction errors, some anonymised words are damaged, and trajectories retrace the report rather than explore. Open side of the decision. When our models leave a case open they often do not name the specific missing evidence, where frontier models are far ahead; and Nautil-RLVR depends less on the evidence than Nautil-SFT.

sections.heading: 8 Conclusion
sections.text: Closing a case only when the evidence supports it is a judgment that does not come with capability: a frontier model finds causes more often than ours and an untrained model about as often, yet both close cases their reports leave undetermined and overstate what the evidence shows. Trained on audited investigation trajectories, a 9B model gains restraint and grounding: its closures move with the evidence, its claims cite what it read, and its conclusions are far less often overstated. A closure-only RL reward lifts accuracy to the teacher’s level at some cost in evidence dependence, whereas rewarding judged conclusion quality collapses the policy into never closing. Because a case’s source can stand in for its evidence, closure accuracy should be reported with a source-only baseline, within sources, and with evidence dependence.

sections.heading: AI use statement
sections.text: In this work, we used generative AI tools for literature search, discussion of research ideas, manuscript editing, and generation of experiment code. We have reviewed all AI-assisted work and take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims and artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

sections.heading: Reproducibility statement
sections.text: Our code repository ( https://github.com/etigerstudio/Nautil ) contains the code, prompts and training configurations of the pipeline, and no data: case extraction for reports, trajectory construction and auditing, splitting and counterfactual construction, the investigation environment, the investigator prompt and tool definition, and the SFT and RLVR code with its reward, judge prompts, configurations and unit tests. The Nautil dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/etigerstudio/Nautil , and the weights of Nautil-SFT and Nautil-RLVR at https://huggingface.co/etigerstudio/Nautil-SFT and https://huggingface.co/etigerstudio/Nautil-RLVR . The production host cases and the code that builds them will be released after internal review.

sections.heading: Sources and licences.
sections.text: Candidate pools: boards 508 reports (ATSB 86, RAIB 158, MAIB 170, CSB 94), NTSB 363 aviation final reports (2014–2024), NHTSA 373 defect investigations, and 1,713 host anomaly windows. ATSB reports are CC BY 4.0, RAIB and MAIB reports are under the Open Government Licence v3, and CSB, NTSB and NHTSA documents are US government works. Host windows were flagged by a rolling median/MAD detector, so they are anomalies, not verified root-cause labels. Medical case reports were not used for training because their licences are mixed; they appear only in the OOD test set.

sections.heading: Report extraction.
sections.text: The extractor (GPT-5.6 Sol) runs seven steps: (1) label each passage as factual, analytical or conclusion; (2) split factual passages into atomic evidence items with neutral titles, moving any sentence that hints at a conclusion to a withheld list; (3) build the source table; (4) write the brief; (5) anonymise; (6) write the hidden reference (determined or not, closure object, official conclusion verbatim, rejected explanations, alternatives left open); (7) review. E 1 E_{1} is regrouped to the first four observation or measurement items of the primary source, so that the opening record does not depend on document layout.

sections.heading: Host textualisation.
sections.text: For each window we select metrics, render one chart per six metrics (baseline median, spread band, largest departure), describe each chart with a vision-language model that also receives the numbers table, and assemble the case with the alert record as E 1 E_{1} . A program flags any number in a description that is not in the table.

sections.heading: Anonymisation.
sections.text: For reports, a model lists identifiers (dates, locations, operators, registrations, report numbers) and a program replaces them in two passes, followed by a forced sweep. The replacement matched substrings rather than whole words, which damaged some ordinary words (e.g. “thunder” became “thundethe”) in at least 63 cases. We did not alter generated trajectories; items never fetched by the teacher were re-anonymised with whole-word matching (942 items). For hosts, service names become neutral roles; IP addresses, alert IDs, links and calendar dates are removed.

sections.heading: Host labels.
sections.text: The JustDiag diagnostic harness ( Bi et al., 2026 ) (with GLM-5.3-Flash) was run on every host window; runs were scored by GPT-5.6 Sol and those scoring ≥ + 1 \geq+1 entered the pool. When writing a host trajectory, the teacher sees this run’s closing report as a reference, so the closure marker of a host trajectory is the teacher’s judgment, not a ground truth. Not-closed host examples come from 79 unfinished diagnosis runs, after removing hosts that also appear in the test set. Rerun under our protocol, the teacher closes only 5 of the 39 host test cases labelled closed, so host labels are not reproducible and host results appear only in Table 13 .

sections.heading: Trajectories and audit.
sections.text: Stage 1 asks the teacher (GPT-6 Sol) for a plan of 3–12 rounds (4–16 for hosts), each with a note, 1–12 new evidence IDs and a reason, and a final answer. A program assembles the dialogue, copying tool returns verbatim, and rejects plans that cite items before they are fetched, use undeclared hypotheses, cite unread items in the final answer, contradict the determined/undetermined reference, or contain withheld identifiers. Stage 2 keeps the prose and fetches, inserts exact-anchor citations, and adds a ledger with states open, favoured and weakened. The audit returns a score from − 5 -5 to + 5 +5 , an action (keep, revise, skip), a hard-failure flag and five checks (source alignment, evidence grounding, active fetching, hypothesis trajectory, honest closure). Funnel over 1,345 non-medical cases: 996 pass Stage 1, 818 pass Stage 2, 458 are kept directly and 60 after one revision of the final answer (518). Adding 21 pilot cases gives 539; we then added 113 supplements (50 host not-closed, 7 oversized board cases, 56 cases wrongly blocked by the identifier check) and 105 failed report cases whose plans were rewritten by a second LLM and then passed the same program checks and audit, and removed 26 board cases whose brief and evidence came from different incidents, for 731.

sections.heading: Splits.
sections.text: The split (seed 20260925) is balanced by source subtype and label and keeps each report incident in one split. Host cases are split by case: 21 of 264 host machines have cases in more than one split (48 cases).

sections.heading: OOD test set.
sections.text: 83 reports (NTSB highway 39, NTSB pipeline 25, TSB Canada pipeline 19, mostly determined), 20 medical cases relabelled by whether the record contains the confirming finding (8 determined, 12 not), 18 microservice faults (one per system and fault type), and 20 Tennessee Eastman runs relabelled by whether the data can identify the fault; 109 should close and 32 should not. Domain predicts label: answering each domain’s majority label, read from the test answers, gives 90.3 balanced accuracy, so we report domains separately (Table 14 ).

sections.heading: Counterfactual versions.
sections.text: The grounds of a case are the evidence items the teacher’s final answer cites as support for its conclusion. Versions remove 40%, 75% or 100% of the grounds; the control removes as many items never cited by the teacher. E 1 E_{1} is never removed, identifiers are not renumbered, and the brief is regenerated with the removed items dropped from the index. A leak check flags removed items whose content is likely restated elsewhere; no edits are made, and the 20 cases without a flagged item in either the 100% or the control version form the leakage-clean subset.

sections.heading: Reference audit.
sections.text: Of 247 references checked, about 10 (4%) contain an extraction error, such as a conclusion field holding a safety notice. We kept them unchanged, since every stage of the pipeline used the same references.

sections.heading: SFT.
sections.text: Qwen3.5-9B, LoRA rank 16, α = 32 \alpha=32 , dropout 0, all linear layers; AdamW, peak learning rate 5 × 10 − 5 5\times 10^{-5} in epoch 1 and 2 × 10 − 5 2\times 10^{-5} in epoch 2 (cosine, 8 warm-up steps), gradient clipping 1.0; batch size 1 per GPU on two H100 GPUs, no packing; 32,768-token sequences in bf16; 273 steps per epoch. The training split has 6.0M tokens, 1.4M of them supervised. Validation cross-entropy after epochs 1–4 is 0.554, 0.537, 0.532 and 0.532; we chose epoch 2 before any test-set use for the reasons in § 5 . We also computed token loss on a 33-case pilot set of teacher trajectories from the OOD domains (lowest at epoch 3, 0.548 vs. 0.549 at epoch 2). All 33 cases belong to the OOD test set, so we do not count this as a selection criterion and report the overlap here. Inference uses vLLM with the unmerged adapter; we verified that the adapter is active by comparing token losses with the training framework.

sections.heading: RLVR.
sections.text: Synchronous GRPO: both GPUs generate with vLLM, which then sleeps while two-GPU data-parallel training runs, and the new adapter is hot-swapped with a loss check. Each step draws 22 cases (8 rollouts each, at least 18 usable groups) and makes 4 AdamW updates; advantages are standardised within groups and groups with identical rewards are dropped; the loss is averaged over sampled assistant tokens. Rollouts use temperature 1.0 in non-thinking mode, 15 turns, 4,096 tokens per turn and 12,000 per case. The training pool has 544 cases (one training case lacked a complete evidence store). Format penalties: no citation − 0.25 -0.25 ; citing unread or non-existent items − 0.5 -0.5 ; each turn beyond six − 0.1 -0.1 (capped at − 1 -1 ); each repeated item beyond ten − 0.1 -0.1 (capped at − 1 -1 ); each malformed call − 0.2 -0.2 (capped at − 1 -1 ); missing marker − 2 -2 .

sections.text: The two judged variants add ( 2 ​ q conc − 1 ) (2q_{\text{conc}}-1) for closed answers and 1 2 ​ ( 2 ​ q conc − 1 ) + 1 2 ​ ( 2 ​ q gap − 1 ) \tfrac{1}{2}(2q_{\text{conc}}-1)+\tfrac{1}{2}(2q_{\text{gap}}-1) for unclosed ones, where q conc q_{\text{conc}} and q gap q_{\text{gap}} come from the checklist of § 3 answered by GPT-6 Luna during training; “always counted” adds this to every rollout, “only if decision right” only when D = + 1 D=+1 . sections.heading: Protocol.
sections.text: Local models run in vLLM (Qwen3.5-9B models with the non-thinking sampling recommended by the model card), 3 samples per case, 15 turns, 4,096 tokens per turn, 12,000 generated tokens per case and a 32k context. API models run through OpenRouter with provider-default sampling and reasoning, reasoning content replayed across turns, 64,000 output tokens per turn and no per-case cap, so that reasoning is not truncated. A run without case closed or case not closed counts as wrong on both sides. Confidence intervals are 95% case bootstraps (5,000 draws) stratified by label (and by source × \times label for within-source accuracy), shared across conditions so that differences are paired.

sections.heading: Judges.
sections.text: GPT-6 Sol judges the first sample of every condition, seeing the final answer, the titles of read and unread items, the text of cited items and the reference (hidden from the investigator), but not the condition name. Hedged statements (“X was not established”) are not counted as claims. When an answer makes no causal claim, the supported-claims item does not apply and the conclusion score averages the other four items. Because Sol is also the teacher, its own investigations are judged by Claude Sonnet 5 (Table 11 ), and 50 stratified requests were re-judged by Sonnet 5 and Grok 4.7 (Table 12 ): conclusion scores correlate at 0.71–0.82, agreement on the cause item is 88% for every pair, and although absolute overstatement rates differ across judges (70%, 28% and 72% overall), all three judges find trained models overstate far less than untrained ones.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.03190v1 [cs.CL] 02 Oct 2026 Not Until the Evidence Says So: Teaching LLM Investigators When to Close a Case Tingzhu Bi Affiliation: Peking University Email: bitingzhu@stu.pku.edu.cn Ping Wang Affiliation: Peking University Email: pwang@pku.edu.cn Meng Ma Affiliation: Peking University Email: mameng@pku.edu.cn Abstract Accident, defect and outage investigations end with a decision that ordinary question answering never faces: whether the evidence gathered so far is enough to close the case. We study this decision for LLM investigators, which request evidence from a case file, revise their hypotheses, and either close the case with a conclusion grounded in what they read or leave it open and name what is missing. This judgment does not come with capability: an untrained 9B model overstates its evidence in 97% of its answers, and a frontier model that identifies the right cause in 84% of cases still overstates in 91% and closes 17 of the 41 cases whose official finding is “cause undetermined”. Measuring it is also non-trivial: the source of a case largely predicts its label, and a rule that reads only the source reaches 83.0 balanced accuracy on our test cases. We therefore evaluate closure with three tests: closure accuracy , reported against this rule and within each source; evidence dependence , which removes the grounds of a conclusion and checks whether the model stops closing; and conclusion and gap quality , a judged checklist of what the model asserts and what it says is missing. We build Nautil, 731 audited cases from aviation, rail, maritime, chemical-safety and vehicle-defect reports and production server incidents, with teacher trajectories, an out-of-distribution test set and counterfactual evidence versions. Fine-tuning a 9B model on these trajectories makes its closures follow the evidence: removing the grounds lowers its closure rate by 26 points relative to a matched control (base model: 6; frontier model: 7), overstatement falls from 97% to 35%, and conclusions that are both correct and not overstated rise from 3% to 43% (frontier model: 9%). Reinforcement learning that rewards only the closure decision then raises balanced accuracy from 69.2 to 83.3, on par with the teacher, and within-source accuracy from 60.4 to 74.1, at some cost in evidence dependence. We release the models, the dataset and the evaluation suite. Dataset: Nautil Models: Nautil-SFT , Nautil-RLVR Demo: Nautil-Demo Code: Nautil 1 Introduction Figure 1: Three investigators on a test case whose official finding is a partial loss of engine power for undetermined reasons . Left: the untrained base model turns an unverified reading into an established engine failure and closes the case. Middle: a frontier model names the power loss that the report establishes and even writes that its cause could not be determined, yet still closes the case. Right: Nautil-SFT keeps the case open and names the missing evidence. Excerpts are the models’ own words, shortened (…); one sample per model. Investigating an aircraft accident, a vehicle defect or a server outage means collecting evidence piece by piece and then deciding whether it is enough to state a cause. Official investigations often decide that it is not: many reports end with “cause undetermined”. An LLM investigator therefore has to make two decisions, not one: what the cause is, and whether the evidence at hand establishes it. Current models are much better at the first decision than at the second (Figure 1 ). On our test cases, a frontier model (Gemini 3.8 Flash) identifies the reference cause in 84% of cases, yet 91% of its answers present as established what the evidence only suggests, and it closes 17 of the 41 cases that the official reports leave undetermined. An untrained 9B model overstates in 97% of its answers. Knowing when to close does not come with the ability to find causes; it has to be taught and measured separately. Abstention research asks whether to answer a single question whose information is given up front ( Kirichenko et al., 2025 ; Zhai et al., 2026 ) , and diagnosis agents are scored on finding the cause ( Xu et al., 2025 ; Pham et al., 2025 ) , not on whether they should have concluded. Our cases hold tens to hundreds of evidence items that must be requested over several turns, and “the cause cannot be determined from this record” is a correct, scored outcome. Measuring this decision is harder than it looks. In real investigation data the source of a case largely predicts its label: most NTSB and NHTSA cases in our data end undetermined, most board and server cases end with a cause. A rule that ignores the evidence and answers by source reaches 83.0 balanced accuracy on our non-host test cases. Any closure accuracy on such data must therefore be read against this rule, within each source, and together with tests that change the evidence while keeping the source fixed. We make four contributions. • Task and evaluation. We define investigative closure and evaluate it with three complementary tests: closure accuracy (reported against the source-only rule and within each source), evidence dependence (counterfactual removal of a conclusion’s grounds against a matched control), and conclusion and gap quality (a judged checklist). • Data. Nautil 1 1 1 Read as not until . contains 731 audited cases from four sources, including real production server incidents, with teacher investigation trajectories, a 141-case out-of-distribution test set and counterfactual evidence versions. • Models. Nautil-SFT and Nautil-RLVR, two 9B investigators. Supervised fine-tuning on audited trajectories makes closure follow the evidence and cuts overstatement; reinforcement learning with a reward on the closure decision alone raises closure accuracy to the teacher’s level. • Findings. Training teaches restraint and grounding rather than cause-finding; rewarding judged conclusion quality during RL collapses the policy into never closing; and an outcome-only reward trades evidence dependence for accuracy. 2 Related Work Abstention and unanswerable questions. Models answer questions they cannot answer ( Rajpurkar et al., 2018 ; Yin et al., 2023 ; Kadavath et al., 2022 ) , even when the context is insufficient ( Joren et al., 2025 ; Kirichenko et al., 2025 ) , partly because binary grading rewards guessing ( Kalai et al., 2025 ) . Abstention has been trained with SFT ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024 ) and RL ( Wei et al., 2026 ; Damani et al., 2026 ; Zhai et al., 2026 ) ; RL fine-tuning can also erode it ( Song et al., 2025b ) , and abstention rewards can collapse into refusal ( Che et al., 2026 ) . Recent work asks models to state what is missing ( Zhai et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2025 ) or to stop acting when they should ( Liu et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . These settings give the information up front and grade whether to answer; in ours, the decision follows multi-turn evidence gathering, and “cannot determine” is set by real investigation reports. LLMs for incident investigation and diagnosis. Root-cause analysis benchmarks and agents for cloud incidents ( Xu et al., 2025 ; Pham et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) , auditable multi-agent diagnosis such as JustDiag ( Bi et al., 2026 ) , evidence-first investigators ( Marozzo and Liò, 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) , and sequential medical diagnosis ( Nori et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2024 ) all score whether the cause is found. Premature closure has been measured in frontier models ( Handler et al., 2026 ) . We add closure itself as a scored, trainable decision across domains. RLVR and agentic RL. Group-relative policy optimisation ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) and tool-using RL agents ( Jin et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2025a ; Wang et al., 2025 ) assume a solvable task with a checkable answer. We make “not closed” one of the verifiable outcomes and show that judge-scored rubric rewards ( Gunjal et al., 2026 ) , which can be gamed ( Skalse et al., 2022 ; Gao et al., 2023 ) , collapse closure in this setting. Shortcuts and faithful evaluation. Annotation artefacts and shortcuts let models score without using the input ( Gururangan et al., 2018 ; Geirhos et al., 2020 ) ; contrast sets and counterfactual edits test whether predictions follow it ( Gardner et al., 2020 ; Kaushik et al., 2020 ) , though constructed insufficiency has its own artefacts ( Qiu et al., 2026 ) . LLM judges are useful but biased, including towards their own outputs ( Zheng et al., 2023 ; Panickssery et al., 2024 ) . These motivate our source-only baseline, matched control and cross-judge checks. 3 Investigative Closure Protocol. An investigator receives a case: a fixed question (what caused the incident, citing evidence for each key claim), a brief, an opening record E 1 E_{1} shown in full (median 4 items), and an index that lists only the identifier and a neutral title of every other evidence item (over all 731 cases: median 115 items per case, up to 682). Titles are written so that they do not reveal conclusions. In each turn the investigator writes a working note (current hypotheses, what the new evidence supports or weakens, a hypothesis ledger, and the next discriminating check) and may call request_evidence for 1–12 unread items; the items arrive in the next message. An episode has at most 15 turns and ends with an answer that starts with case closed , followed by a causal conclusion that cites the evidence, or case not closed , followed by what is established, what is missing, and a provisional assessment. The label of a report case is whether the official report determined the cause at the level its investigation pursued (the closure object in the reference); a report that establishes an event, such as a loss of engine power, but not its cause leaves the case open. Three tests. A single accuracy can be inflated either by the source of a case or by a conservative policy, so we evaluate closure with three tests, each closing one loophole: closure accuracy guards against recognising the source instead of reading the evidence; evidence dependence guards against closing out of habit, or stopping merely because evidence is scarce; and conclusion and gap quality guards against a right decision with a wrong or overstated conclusion. Closure accuracy. We report the rate of closing among cases that should close, the rate of not closing among cases that should not, and their mean (balanced accuracy), so that never closing is not rewarded. An answer without a closure marker counts as wrong on both sides. Every result is shown next to the source-only rule , which gives each source its majority training label. Within-source balanced accuracy computes balanced accuracy separately inside each report source and averages them; the source-only rule scores exactly 50 on it, so only reading the evidence can raise it. Evidence dependence. For cases labelled closed, we build a version without the items the conclusion rests on and a control without the same number of other items; the brief and question are unchanged, and removed items simply drop out of the index. The two versions differ only in whether the grounds are present, so the source is held fixed. We report the difference in closure rate between them (removed minus control; more negative means closure follows the evidence) and a two-class balanced accuracy per case, 1 2 ​ [ 𝟙 ​ ( control closed ) + 𝟙 ​ ( removed explicitly not closed ) ] \tfrac{1}{2}[\mathbb{1}(\text{control closed})+\mathbb{1}(\text{removed explicitly not closed})] . Conclusion and gap quality. A judge answers a fixed checklist about the final answer against the reference: whether the initiating cause is right, whether the causal chain matches, whether the answer overstates (presents as established what the evidence only suggests), what share of its causal claims cite evidence that was read and supports them, and whether it addresses alternative explanations. Our summary metric is the share of answers whose cause is right and not overstated. For unclosed answers the judge also checks whether the gap names specific evidence, whether that evidence is truly absent from the case, and whether it matches the reference’s reason for indeterminacy. The main judge is GPT-6 Sol; because it is also the teacher (§ 4 ), we repeat the checklist with Claude Sonnet 5 and Grok 4.7 (§ 6.3 , Appendix C ). 4 The Nautil Dataset Figure 2: Overview of Nautil. (1) Case files are built from four sources: evidence items with neutral titles are shown on demand, conclusions are withheld, and a hidden reference records whether the case should close; counterfactual versions and the OOD set follow the same format. (2) The teacher plans each investigation from the report and its label, a program assembles and checks it, Stage 2 adds citations and the hypothesis ledger, and audited trajectories train Nautil-SFT. (3) RLVR rewards only the closure decision, checked by a program. Right: one round of an actual Nautil-SFT investigation on a test case whose official finding is undetermined; after its checks weaken the fuel and engine explanations, it leaves the case open. Sources. Nautil draws on four kinds of investigation (Table 1 ). Boards : reports of four transport and chemical-safety boards (ATSB, RAIB, MAIB, CSB). NTSB : aviation final reports 2014–2024. NHTSA : vehicle defect investigations, with opening and closing summaries. Host : anomaly windows from a year of production server monitoring at a large internet company. Report cases take their label from whether the official report determined the cause. Host incidents have no report; their label is the teacher’s closure decision (below), which we use for training and report only in the appendix. Case files. For reports, an extraction pipeline (GPT-5.6 Sol) splits the text into factual, analytical and conclusion passages, turns factual passages into atomic evidence items with neutral titles, withholds any sentence that hints at the conclusion, writes the brief, anonymises identifiers, and records a hidden reference: whether the cause was determined, the official conclusion, rejected explanations and alternatives left open. E 1 E_{1} is fixed to the first four observation or measurement items of the primary source. For hosts, selected metric series are rendered as charts and described in text by a vision-language model that sees each chart with its numbers table and may quote only those numbers; a program flags any number not in the table. Service names are replaced by neutral roles, and addresses, alert IDs and dates are removed. Teacher trajectories. The teacher (GPT-6 Sol) sees the case file, the official analysis and the label, and plans an investigation: per turn, a note, the items to request and why, then a final answer (Stage 1). A program assembles the dialogue with tool returns copied verbatim, rejecting plans that cite unrequested items, contradict the label or leak withheld identifiers. Stage 2 adds exact citations and a ledger marking each hypothesis open, favoured or weakened, with every change citing visible evidence. For hosts the teacher also sees the closing report of a run of the JustDiag diagnostic harness ( Bi et al., 2026 ) on the incident. Trajectories are retraced from the report’s argument; their fetch order is not free exploration. Audit. The teacher scores each trajectory from − 5 -5 to + 5 +5 on alignment with the source, evidence grounding, active fetching, hypothesis updates and honest closure; we keep scores ≥ 4 \geq 4 without hard failures and allow one revision of the final answer for + 3 +3 . Of 1,345 generated report and host cases, 996 pass Stage 1, 818 pass Stage 2 and 518 (38.5%) pass the audit; with supplements for host not-closed cases, a salvage round and the removal of 26 cases whose brief and evidence came from different incidents, the final set has 731 cases. It is split 545 / 74 / 112 within each source, balancing labels and keeping each incident in one split. Table 1: Nautil by source. Items: median evidence items per case, over all cases of the source. Source Candidates Cases Closed / not closed Items Train / Val / Test Boards (4 agencies) 508 140 110 / 30 173 102 / 15 / 23 NTSB (aviation) 363 142 19 / 123 23.5 107 / 14 / 21 NHTSA (vehicle defects) 373 130 7 / 123 26 97 / 13 / 20 Host (servers) 1,713 319 259 / 60 145 239 / 32 / 48 Total 731 395 / 336 115 545 / 74 / 112 Source and label. Table 1 shows the structure that makes closure hard to measure: boards and hosts mostly close, NTSB and NHTSA mostly do not. Answering by source alone gives 83.0 balanced accuracy on the 64 non-host test cases (23 should close, 41 should not). This is why every closure result below is paired with the source-only rule and the within-source metric, and why the headline test set is non-host: host labels are teacher judgments, and the teacher itself, rerun under the same protocol, closes only 5 of the 39 host test cases labelled closed. Out-of-distribution test set. 141 cases from unseen domains: 83 reports (NTSB highway and pipeline, TSB Canada pipeline), 20 medical cases ( Wu et al., 2025 ) relabelled by whether the record contains the confirming finding, 18 microservice faults ( Pham et al., 2025 ) , and 20 Tennessee Eastman process runs ( Downs and Vogel, 1993 ; Rieth et al., 2017 ) . Domain and label are again tied, so we report the OOD set per domain and as a secondary column. Counterfactual versions. For the 62 test cases the teacher closes, the grounds are the items its final answer cites; versions remove 40%, 75% or 100% of them, and the control removes as many other items. A leak check flags removed items that may be restated elsewhere; 20 cases have none. 5 Training Nautil Investigators Supervised fine-tuning. We fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B ( Qwen Team, 2026 ) with LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) (rank 16, α = 32 \alpha=32 , all linear layers) on the 545 training trajectories, with the native tool-call format, a 32k-token context, and loss on assistant turns only. We train two epochs (546 steps) and select the epoch-2 checkpoint before touching the test set: validation loss flattens after it, validation closure accuracy is highest, and its samples disagree most on the closure decision, which leaves room for RL. We call it Nautil-SFT. RLVR with a closure-only reward. Starting from Nautil-SFT, we run GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) in the same case environment. ReAct prompting (47.7) and our ledger format as a prompt (55.3, with 95% overstatement) leave the base model’s closing habit intact (Table 2 ). Abstain-R1 (27.9) and its base model (39.2) mostly fail to finish a multi-turn investigation (44% and 32% of runs end without a closure marker): abstention learned on single questions does not carry over to evidence gathering. Out of distribution and long files. OOD balanced accuracy rises from 50.6 (base) to 61.7 (Nautil-SFT) and 67.0 (Nautil-RLVR), close to Gemini (68.9). Because domain and label are tied in this set, this mostly reflects the direction of the decision; within individual domains no model is clearly above chance (Appendix D ). On the 20 largest files, Nautil-RLVR closes 93% of should-close cases when fetching its own evidence and 61% when given the whole file, which in turn matches the main cause more often (Appendix E ). The source of a case still predicts its label, so accuracy is paired with within-source and counterfactual tests; the within-source metric rests mostly on board cases. Host labels are teacher judgments the teacher does not reproduce; host results are in the appendix. Judge, teacher and samples. GPT-6 Sol is both teacher and main judge, so its investigator row is only a reference; two further judges agree on direction but not on absolute rates. API models are mostly sampled once; the non-host counterfactual set has 23 cases, and its grounds are defined by the teacher’s citations. The Nautil-RLVR checkpoint was screened on 30 test cases, and a 33-case pilot set consulted while choosing the SFT epoch overlaps the OOD test set. Data. About 4% of references have extraction errors, some anonymised words are damaged, and trajectories retrace the report rather than explore. Open side of the decision. When our models leave a case open they often do not name the specific missing evidence, where frontier models are far ahead; and Nautil-RLVR depends less on the evidence than Nautil-SFT. 8 Conclusion Closing a case only when the evidence supports it is a judgment that does not come with capability: a frontier model finds causes more often than ours and an untrained model about as often, yet both close cases their reports leave undetermined and overstate what the evidence shows. Trained on audited investigation trajectories, a 9B model gains restraint and grounding: its closures move with the evidence, its claims cite what it read, and its conclusions are far less often overstated. A closure-only RL reward lifts accuracy to the teacher’s level at some cost in evidence dependence, whereas rewarding judged conclusion quality collapses the policy into never closing. Because a case’s source can stand in for its evidence, closure accuracy should be reported with a source-only baseline, within sources, and with evidence dependence.
